questions.q: Why is Local System considered a poor choice for a production SQL Server service account?
options: It doesn't allow SQL Server to start at all
It's only available on Linux installations
It requires a domain to function
It's the most privileged built-in account and a shared identity with no accountability to a specific service
questions.explain: Local System grants far more machine-level privilege than the service needs, with no way to audit which service used it.

questions.q: What makes a group Managed Service Account (gMSA) the current best practice on a domain?
options: It only works with SQL Server Express
It is identical in privilege to Local System but easier to type
It has no password at all and requires no domain
It behaves as a least-privilege, individually-auditable identity while Active Directory rotates its password automatically
questions.explain: A gMSA removes the manual password-rotation burden a plain dedicated domain account carries, without giving up least-privilege benefits.

questions.q: Why should you change a SQL Server service account through Configuration Manager rather than services.msc?
options: Configuration Manager is required by Windows for all services, not just SQL Server
Configuration Manager also grants the account the right to act as a service and adjusts registry/file permissions the change depends on
There is no real difference; either approach works identically
services.msc is not able to change any service's account at all
questions.explain: Changing the account directly in services.msc can leave the instance in a broken state because the necessary permission grants weren't applied.

questions.q: What is SQL Server Configuration Manager's actual job?
options: Managing SQL Server Agent job schedules
Managing SQL Server services and network protocol configuration for every installed instance and component on a machine
Managing Windows Update settings
Writing and executing T-SQL queries against a database
questions.explain: It's a dedicated MMC snap-in for service and network management, separate from SQL Server Management Studio, which is for T-SQL and object management.

questions.q: Which network protocol is the standard for real client-server SQL Server connectivity and must be enabled for anything beyond local connections?
options: TCP/IP
Shared Memory
HTTP
Named Pipes
questions.explain: Shared Memory only works for connections originating on the same machine, and Named Pipes is mostly used for local/same-machine scenarios; TCP/IP is needed for real network client-server connectivity.
